opus-5.5.text:
I think the value is enormous, and it really comes down to scale and accessibility. If you look at how reinforcement learning has traditionally worked, agents learn by interacting with an environment, often for millions of steps, and that interaction is expensive. In simulation it costs compute, and in the real world, on a robot, it's slow, it can be unsafe, and the hardware wears out. So one of the big questions I've been interested in is: how can we give agents some prior knowledge about the world before they ever start acting in it?

Videos are a really natural answer to that. There is an incredible amount of video data out there of people cooking, playing games, assembling furniture, driving, doing all sorts of tasks. That data implicitly contains a lot of information about how the world works and about what good behavior looks like. The challenge is that videos are observation-only. You see what happens, but you don't see the actions that were taken. You don't know which buttons someone pressed or what torques a person applied with their muscles. So you can't just plug them into standard imitation learning, which usually assumes you have state-action pairs.

A lot of my work has been about trying to bridge that gap, for example by learning latent actions from observations alone. The idea is that even if you don't know the true actions, you can infer some latent representation of what caused one frame to transition to the next. Then you can learn a policy over those latent actions from the videos, and only afterward use a small amount of real environment interaction to figure out how those latent actions map to the agent's actual actions. That way, most of the learning happens offline from cheap, abundant data, and you only need a little bit of costly interaction to ground it.

Beyond policies, videos are also useful for learning reward functions, which is often the hardest part of applying RL in practice. Hand-designing a reward that captures what you actually want is notoriously tricky. If you can watch demonstrations of a task and infer what progress toward the goal looks like, you can give the agent a much more informative signal than a sparse success-or-failure reward.

Then there's the broader vision, which is how humans learn. We learn so much by watching others. A child can watch someone open a door and then try it themselves, even though they've never been told which muscles to move. If we want agents that are more general and more sample-efficient, I think learning from observation, and from video in particular, is going to be a core ingredient. It's not a complete solution on its own, since you still need interaction to correct mistakes and handle differences between the demonstrator and the agent, but as a source of prior knowledge it's one of the most promising directions we have.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core of it is that videos are just an enormous, cheap source of information about how the world works, and reinforcement learning has historically ignored most of it. When we train an agent in the usual way, it has to collect all of its own experience through trial and error, and that's expensive. Meanwhile there are millions of hours of video on the internet of people doing things: cooking, playing games, assembling furniture, walking around. Humans learn a tremendous amount just by watching, and it felt strange to me that our agents couldn't.

The catch is that video doesn't come with actions or rewards. You see the frames change, but you don't see the controller inputs or the motor commands that caused those changes. So a lot of my work has been about asking, what can you still learn from observation alone? One answer is that you can learn a notion of progress, or value. If you watch a demonstration, frames near the end of a successful task tend to look like "closer to done" than frames at the beginning, so you can learn a reward signal purely from watching, and then use that to guide an agent that does have access to its own actions. That was the idea behind some of our imitation-from-observation work.

The other direction, which I've become more excited about, is learning the actions themselves in a latent sense. Even if you don't know what button was pressed, you can look at two consecutive frames and infer that something happened between them, and you can learn a compact, discrete representation of that "something." Once you have that, video becomes a kind of action-labeled dataset for free. You can train policies on it, you can build world models that let you imagine consequences, and then it only takes a small amount of real interaction to ground those latent actions into the actual control space of a particular robot or game.

So the way I see the value is really about scale and generality. Simulators are great but they're narrow, and real-world interaction is slow. Video sits in between: it's diverse, it's abundant, and it reflects the real distribution of things people actually do. If we can get agents to extract priors about dynamics and about what goals look like from that, then the hard reinforcement learning part becomes much smaller. You're fine-tuning rather than learning from scratch. I think that's how you eventually get agents that generalize across many tasks and environments rather than being retrained for each one.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting thing about learning from videos is that we have so much information about how to do things without necessarily having the actions that produced those behaviors. If you watch someone perform a task, you can see what changes in the environment, but you don’t have access to the commands they sent to their muscles or, in the case of a robot, its motors.

That’s a challenge for a lot of imitation learning approaches, which typically assume you have both observations and actions. So the question is: can we learn something useful from those observations alone, and then use that to help an agent learn how to act?

For reinforcement learning, that could make exploration much more directed. Instead of starting from scratch, the agent has some indication of what successful behavior looks like. It still needs to interact with its environment and figure out which actions produce those outcomes, but video can provide a useful starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think videos are a really exciting source of information because they show us how people interact with the world. In reinforcement learning, an agent typically has to learn through its own trial and error, and that can require a lot of experience. With video, we can ask whether some of that learning can happen simply by observing someone else.

The challenge is that a video usually doesn’t tell you what actions were taken or what rewards the person received. You see how the world changes, but you don’t have all the information a reinforcement learning algorithm would normally use. So the question becomes: what can we extract from those observations to help an agent learn?

Even if observation doesn’t completely replace interaction, it could give the agent a useful starting point—an idea of what successful behavior looks like—so it doesn’t have to discover everything from scratch.
